commit message:
refactor(core): Merge filestream "loop_" files

Description
---
Merges `loop_process.go`, `loop_transmit.go` and `loop_feedback.go` into a single `filestreamimpl.go` (open to naming suggestions). This makes the data flow a bit easier to see. One can think of these three goroutines as a single function that processes Updates, so it helps to see all the processing steps an Update undergoes in one place.

I also made each `loop` function close its corresponding output stream on its own so that channels are closed near where they're pushed to. As a side effect, this simplifies `filestream.Close()`.

This allows me to delete the `func-mitm-py*` and `func-docs-py*` tox environments. I can't delete `func-base-py*` yet because it's used by a Windows job, and I don't want to debug Windows at this moment.

Replaces `nox-tests` by `nox-tests-linux`, `nox-tests-macos` and `nox-tests-win` so that invocations don't have to pass an executor and duplicate the corresponding `install_deps` parameter.

Fixes all Windows test jobs ([WB-18423](https://wandb.atlassian.net/browse/WB-18423)) by figuring out how to install Python properly. The package on Chocolatey is bad at unattended installation.

commit message:
fix(wandb): add support for gymnasium v0.29.1+ and handle version-based API changes

- Added `_gymnasium_version_gt_0_29_1` global variable to track gymnasium version.
- Updated `monitor` function to handle new `RecordVideo` API introduced in gymnasium v0.29.1+.
- Maintained compatibility with gym versions <0.26.0 by conditionally setting `path` and `recorder`.
- Patched appropriate video recorder based on the detected version of gym or gymnasium.
- Ensured proper cleanup and logging of video recordings.

This commit ensures that the wandb integration works seamlessly with both older and newer versions of gym and gymnasium libraries.

commit message:
fix(wandb): use getattr to dynamically fetch RecordVideo wrapper for gymnasium

- Changed from directly importing RecordVideo to using `getattr` to dynamically fetch the `RecordVideo` wrapper.
- Ensured compatibility with gymnasium v0.29.1+ by modifying how the `RecordVideo` class is accessed.

This update ensures a more flexible and error-free way of accessing the `RecordVideo` wrapper for newer gymnasium versions.

author: Drew Meyers <drewhmeyers@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix(wandb/gymnasium): ensure compatibility with gymnasium v1.0.0 and gym <0.26

- Added support for gymnasium v1.0.0 by checking for the new `RecordVideo` wrapper.
- Maintained backward compatibility with older versions of gym and gymnasium.
- Implemented conditional logic to handle the breaking changes in gym 0.26.0.
- Updated `_gymnasium_version_lt_1_0_0` to check for gymnasium versions less than 1.0.0.
- Refactored the `close` function to include conditional logic for both new and old APIs.

commit message:
fix(core): Correctly sample history metrics with nested keys

Description
---
The sampler implementation in `handler.go` was not reading the `NestedKey` field of `HistoryItem`. This pulls out history sampling logic into a dedicated `runhistorysampler.go` file and implements it properly.

There is a bug in Python where it doesn't _read_ the `nested_key` field. I left a comment about it in `runhistorysampler.go`. Amazingly, this is countered by a bug in the Python TensorBoard integration, which seems to produce items that use `key` instead of `nested_key`, causing them to have sparklines anyway.

Testing
---
The following doesn't print a sparkline with the Python implementation but does with `wandb.require("core")`:

```python
with wandb.init() as run:
    for x in range(100):
        run.log({"my": {"value": x}})
```

The TensorBoard integration with and without core prints sparklines.

commit message:
feat(core): Lower rate-limit and better batching in filestream

Description
---
Send at most one filestream request per 15 seconds and accumulate data while waiting.

I broke out `TransmitLoop` and `CollectLoop` out of `filestreamimpl.go` because testing it thoroughly was becoming a pain.

Fixes WB-19169 (but see note below).

This solves two problems:

1. We're less likely to overload the backend with too many small requests
2. On a slow network, we'll send fewer, larger requests
    * Before, we would have sent the same requests but slower
    * Before, filestream could easily clog up, causing the service to not handle any new messages until requests go through

NOTE: There's no request size cap. In extreme cases, `filestream` may accumulate a request so large that it will never succeed. I plan to implement this later.

Testing
---
Manually run the following with debug logging:

```python
import time
from tqdm import trange
import wandb

with wandb.init() as run:
    for i in trange(60):
        run.log({"i": i})
        time.sleep(1)
```

Then examine the posted requests:

```
jq '
  select(.msg | contains("filestream: post request"))
    | [.time, (.request | fromjson)]
' wandb/latest-run/logs/debug-internal.log
```

The requests are spaced 15 seconds apart except for the last one.

commit message:
fix(sdk): Don't os._exit() if internal process had non-zero exit code

Description
---
Instead of calling `os._exit()`, calls `sys.exit()`---ensuring that it does not happen inside an `atexit` hook.

I kept the current behavior of exiting the process on teardown() if the internal process exits with a non-zero code, but it feels like a terrible semantic that we should reconsider.

I looked for uses of `_teardown` by doing a regex search using `\._teardown\(`; `wandb_setup` is the only place that invoked this.

Testing
---
In my PR that enables Go race detection, using `sys.exit()` makes tests fail when there's a data race rather than quitting pytest and sending pytest-xdist into a "worker crashed" loop.

commit message:
refactor(core): Fix race condition in FileTransferManager

Description
---
Simplifies `FileTransferManager` and gets rid of a race condition in the old implementation due to the `active` field.

The race condition was caused by setting `fm.active` to true inside the goroutine started by `Start`. The race happened between `Start()` being called by `Sender.sendRequestDownloadArtifact()` and `Close()` being called by `Sender.sendRequestDefer()`.

This race could cause `Close()` to not wait for all uploads/downloads to finish.

`active`, `inChan` and `Start()` were unnecessary. We can start task goroutines in `AddTask()` directly.

Testing
---
System tests for artifacts running in CI provide good coverage of the `sendRequestDownloadArtifact()` path which is how we found the race. I rebased https://github.com/wandb/wandb/pull/7862 onto this PR to verify that the race is fixed.

commit message:
refactor(core): Define FileStreamRequest, delete CollectorState

Description
---
Replaces "CollectorState" / "FsTransmitData" and cleans up that whole mess.

To review, read `filestreamrequest.go` where most of the work happens.

I define following types:

* `FileStreamRequest`
* `FileStreamRequestJSON`
* `FileStreamRequestReader`
* `FileStreamState`

An important property of filestream is that any sequence of requests can be compressed into one request. This wasn't well represented by the old abstractions. Now, there is a `FileStreamRequest` type with a `Merge()` method.

The `FileStreamRequest` represents a request for an idealized API; on the other hand, `FileStreamRequestJSON` is the reality we live in:

* Some requests can't _actually_ be combined. The filestream API doesn't allow us to update nonconsecutive lines in a file in one request, which happens when we perform terminal emulation.
* When that happens, we break the idealized request into multiple smaller requests. But in doing so, we must preserve an ordering guarantee: the run's exit code must only be set in the final request.

`FileStreamRequestReader`: The `FileStreamRequest` struct is well-suited for quick merge operations, but breaking it into a `FileStreamRequestJSON` "head" and a `FileStreamRequest` "tail" (containing any remaining data) requires memory copy operations. If we're unlucky, this could be a lot of work---like if we buffered a very large request. The Reader defers this work until we actually need it instead of repeating it each time we merge a request into the buffer. Concretely, we avoid unnecessary copying while waiting for rate limits (1 request / 15 sec) or the previous network operation to complete. Copying is necessary because request buffering must happen in a different goroutine than sending.

`FileStreamState`: This is state that would ideally exist on the backend. It's kept separate from the idealized `FileStreamRequest`, but we need it to create the real `FileStreamRequestJSON` values. It's stuff like a console line offset for appending logs to a resumed run, or the next history line number (since we always append to history).

Testing
---
It was easy to write thorough `FileStreamRequest` unit tests which speaks to its success as a model :)

Some manual testing as well:

```python
import time
import sys

from tqdm import tqdm, trange
import wandb

run = wandb.init()

for i in trange(60):
    # Exercise console logging. This forces tqdm to send out
    # ANSI escape sequences to the terminal.
    tqdm.write(f"Iteration {i}:")

    # Exercise history + summary and buffering behaviors:
    for j in trange(1000):
        run.log({"i": i, "j": j})
        # Wait to exercise system metrics logic and also
        # rate-limiting and buffering.
        time.sleep(1.0 / 1000.0)

sys.exit(1)
```

It's hard to manually test the UploadedFiles and Preempting parts. If you run with WANDB_CORE_DEBUG=true, you can see that all standard files appear in the "uploaded" field of a filestream request at some point:

```
jq '
  select(.msg|contains("filestream: post request")) |
  .request | fromjson |
  .uploaded
' wandb/debug-internal.log
```

commit message:
feat(core): Limit filestream request size

Description
---
Fixes WB-19414.

Sets a limit of ~10MB for individual filestream requests. If we accumulate 10MB of data, we send it immediately.

The intention is to avoid accidentally accumulating a request that's too large to be sent successfully, like if the user loses internet connection and accumulates a lot of `run.log()` calls.

Testing
---
```python
from tqdm import trange
import wandb

with wandb.init(project="timoffex-testing", entity="timoffex") as run:
    for i in trange(1000000):
        run.log({
            "x": 1,
            "y": 2,
            "z": 3,
            "a": 4,
        })
```

Run with WANDB_CORE_DEBUG=true and then use

```
grep "filestream: post request" wandb/debug-internal.log |
  jq '.request | length'
```

to check the resulting requests and their sizes. They're all around 12e6. Warning: this logs ~3GB of data!

commit message:
refactor(core): stdlib json in artifacts / launch code, plus cleanup

Description
---
Replaces segmentio-encoding/json by standard Go json in several places.

Summary of changes:

* `job_builder.go`: json is only used for the "metadata" file, which I believe cannot have infs or NaNs
* Refactored `job_builder.go::buildArtifact` to not use json to convert a struct to a map, but instead to pass the struct directly to `artifactBuilder.AddData`, which I changed to accept `any` JSON-encodable value rather than a map
* `manifest.go`: json is only used for the "manifest" struct, which doesn't contain any floats (other than potentially in the "Extra" field of a "Contents" entry)
* `files.go`: json is only used in `WriteJsonToFileWithDigest` which is only used by the code above

Reviewers: #mlw-team, kptkin

Reviewed By: kptkin

Pull Request: https://github.com/wandb/wandb/pull/7933

commit message:
refactor(core): Replace segmentio-encoding/json

Description
---
Replaces segmentio-encoding/json by wandb/simplejsonext (which is necessary to support encoding/decoding Infinity and NaN; otherwise we'd use the standard json package).

NOTE: There are important semantic differences that could cause issues. I tried to be careful, but we might get unexpected behavior in places that are not well tested. Here are a few errors that caught me off guard:

* JSON numbers are always unmarshalled as either `int64` or `float64`. ~There was system metrics code that asserted that numbers were `float64` (which works for `encoding/json`, I think) which resulted in panics.~ (updated: system metrics can use `encoding/json`, but I left some of the cleanup that I did)
* Only string-keyed maps can be marshalled to JSON. I had to modify `runconfig.go` because it was using an int-keyed map for telemetry and "metrics".
* `{}` is unmarshalled as a `nil` map. I had to check for this case in a few spots.

commit message:
refactor(core): Rewrite runsummary and runmetric

Description
---

Fixes: WB-19723

Untangles `runsummary` and `runmetric` from each other and gets rid of all sorts of hacks including some surprising dependencies between `handler` and `sender`.

This improves some `define_metric` behaviors in `wandb-core`. For instance,

```python
with wandb.init() as run:
    run.define_metric("a.b", summary="mean")
    run.log({"a": {"b": 1}})
    run.log({"a": {"b": 2}})
    run.log({"a": {"b": 3}})
```

causes the run's summary to include `a.b.mean: 2`. This also works with globs (`define_metric("a.*.b")`). However, this does not work when using `run.log({"a.b": ...})`---a `.`-separated key always identifies a nested value.

Testing
---
In addition to the existing test suite, thorough manual tests including:

* Simple `run.log()` statements, followed by checking the overview page summary and uploaded summary file
* Various `run.define_metric()` patterns including using multiple calls to define one metric
* Interacting with `run.summary`

commit message:
chore(sdk): communicate_status => deliver_status

Description
---
Replaces `communicate_status()`, which uses the deprecated "communicate" verb and MessageRouter path, by `deliver_status()` which uses the newer Mailbox.

This changes a method in `streams.py` to wait indefinitely rather than with a 5s timeout. Users that previously hit the `AssertionError` in that method will now see either:

* A success, if the 5s timeout was just not enough (what we expect)
* A hanging process, if a response was never going to happen. This would be a bug.

We do not currently have a mechanism to propagate deadlines, but it would be more appropriate than using an indefinite timeout. The goal of this PR is to replace a deprecated codepath.

Testing
---
A simple `wandb.init()` script with `WANDB__REQUIRE_CORE=false` to trigger the `streams.py` change.

I grepped for "communicate_status" in the codebase to find all usages.

This plugin is quite old and not updated to TF 2.0 unfortunately, but we had support for it before wandb-core and people seem to use it. There's some documentation available in https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorboard/blob/master/tensorboard/plugins/pr_curve/README.md, and to use it with TensorFlow 2 you must use the trick here: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorboard/issues/2902#issuecomment-551301396

Visible differences from non-core:

* The table is stored as a file rather than as an artifact
* There's no autogenerated chart showing the table summary
  * I'm not sure yet where this chart comes from

Testing
---
Manually testing this codepath is simple and doesn't require running any heavy computations:

```python
import tensorboard.summary.v1 as tb_summary
import tensorflow as tf
import wandb

with wandb.init(sync_tensorboard=True) as run:
    writer = tf.summary.create_file_writer("tblogdir")
    with writer.as_default():
        # Test the "scalars" path.
        tf.summary.scalar("loss", 0.345, step=1)
        tf.summary.scalar("loss", 0.234, step=2)
        tf.summary.scalar("loss", 0.123, step=3)

        # Test the "pr_curves" path.
        # Workaround described in GH issue mentioned in PR.
        tf.summary.experimental.write_raw_pb(
            tb_summary.pr_curve(
                "pr",
                labels=tf.constant([True, True, False, False]),
                predictions=tf.constant([0.9, 0.8, 0.2, 0.1]),
                num_thresholds=4,
            ),
            step=3,
        )
```

This could be made into a functional test, but I ran into issues with `yea` trying to get it to work.

commit message:
chore(sdk): change TB metric naming in legacy service

Description
---
Removes the strange case where, if you log "x" to a directory called "logdir", then you'll get a metric "logdir/x" in W&B, but if the directory is called "experiment", then you'll get a metric called "experiment" rather than "experiment/x".

It appears this was added to produce nicer names with tensorboardX, but it creates unexpected inconsistencies for other TB logging patterns. It's not clear if anyone ever relied on this.

Reviewers: kptkin

Reviewed By: kptkin

Pull Request: https://github.com/wandb/wandb/pull/8313

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: move some config initialization out of wandb_run.py (#9320)

Instead of initializing `_wandb/code_path` and `_wandb/branch_point` in `Run._init`, do it in `_WandbInit.make_run_config`.

# Safety

Their values depend solely on settings, which are finalized by the time `make_run_config` is called. The `result.base_no_artifacts` dict at the end of `_WandbInit.make_run_config` is the `config` dict at the start of `Run._init`---no changes to the config happen in between. Nothing in-between those calls depends on the config values either.

The only semantic change is that now, a disabled run will have the `_wandb` key in its config because `make_disabled_run` uses the result of `make_run_config`.

# Purpose

The `Run` constructor takes three "config" parameters and merges them into its `Config` object. These values cannot be combined and passed as one dict because the keys from `sweep_config` and `launch_config` must become "locked".

The `sweep_config` and `launch_config` parameters are not used outside of this because they are initialization concepts, not `Run` concepts.

`Run` should construct its own `Config`, since `Config` holds a back-reference to the `Run` and is therefore a part of `Run` rather than something that can exist independently---i.e. `Run` shouldn't accept a `Config` object in its constructor.

Since `Config` is mutable, an easy simplification is to initialize the `Run` with an empty `Config` and update it after which is where I'm trying to go with these PRs.

commit message:
refactor: replace mailbox.ContextCancelledError (#9365)

Replace `mailbox.ContextCancelledError` by `retry.RetryCancelledError`.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix: break connection on parsing error (#9391)

When failing to unmarshal data on an incoming connection in `wandb-core`, stop reading the connection and shut down the server, as future data may be invalid.

I cleaned up the `context` management a little bit. `main.go` no longer creates a context as the `observability.Commit` value was unused.

Breaking the loop closes `inChan`, which causes `handleIncomingRequests()` to end its loop and close `outChan`, which causes `processOutgoingData()` to end its loop.

Simultaneously, `ManageConnectionData()` will close the TCP connection---which may cause `processOutgoingData()` to log errors---and return. Any other connections will do the same, possibly logging errors in `processIncomingData()`, and after this the server will exit.

Any remaining clients will raise errors when sending requests or reading responses, which would most likely manifest as `run` methods like `run.log()` raising a `BrokenPipeError` (or `SockClientClosedError`, maybe).

commit message:
refactor: asyncio compatibility tools (#9379)

Adds `asyncio_compat.py` file with some important utilities for using `asyncio` safely.

In `asyncio`, cancelling a task does not cancel subtasks that it started. Python 3.11 adds a `TaskGroup` class to fix this, but we need custom code for Python 3.8 - 3.10.

Using `asyncio.run` inside an `asyncio` event loop is not allowed. In case any of our users call `wandb` functions in an `asyncio` context, the `asyncio_compat.run` function starts an `asyncio` loop in a new thread.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: new mailbox implementation (#9380)

A reimplementation of `mailbox.py` with tests and documentation, that works with `asyncio`.

This PR does not delete the old mailbox, and no code uses the new mailbox yet.

## Design notes

The `MailboxProbe` / `MailboxProgress` mechanism in the old implementation relied heavily on callbacks and was undocumented / untyped making it difficult to use. The new mailbox provides an async interface for the same purpose, see PR #9382.

The `wait()` method on `MailboxHandle` is there for compatibility with old code, so that it's possible to migrate incrementally.

The old mailbox's "keepalive" mechanism is replaced by a `Mailbox.close()` method which the Router is meant to call when it stops reading new messages (in a `finally` block).

## test_new_mailbox.py

The test file is a little repetitive because it tests both the sync (`wait_or`) and async (`wait_async`) versions of the same functionality. Most tests are short and simple, but the `test_unblocks_wait_*` tests are more involved as they attempt to test concurrency.

I don't call it `test_mailbox.py` because `pytest` doesn't like when multiple test files have the same name (even in different directories). I'll rename it after deleting the old mailbox.

commit message:
refactor: mailbox wait_with_progress (#9382)

Implements `wait_with_progress`, which replaces the old  `MailboxProbe` / `MailboxProgress` mechanism.

Basic usage:

```python
async def display_progress() -> NoReturn:
    # This function never returns. It is cancelled by wait_with_progress
    # on timeout or when the handle gets a result or is abandoned.
    while True:
        update_screen()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

wait_with_progress(
    handle,
    timeout=30,
    progress_after=1,
    display_progress=display_progress,
)
```

Using `asyncio` allows `display_progress` to poll (e.g. RequestPollExit) and update the screen simultaneously---at independent rates!---by starting two tasks (not shown above).

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: replace old mailbox with new mailbox (#9420)

Deletes the old mailbox implementation and updates all code to use the new one.

Nice side effect: the spinners shown in `run.finish()` now update 10 times per second instead of once every second. We still only poll once a second.

The new `MailboxHandle.wait` method has the same semantics as the old one, so I did not update it in this PR. This PR only updates code that used the old `on_probe`/`on_progress`/`wait_all` functionality.

The new mailbox does not have a "keepalive" flag. In the old mailbox, handles created with this flag would periodically generate KeepAlive requests in `wait()` and use this to detect when the connection to the service process is closed. Instead, the Router object that delivers responses to it calls `mailbox.close()` when it is done, which also happens if the connection to the internal service process closes.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: delete deprecated handle wait (#9421)

Deletes the `MailboxHandle.wait()` method and replaces all uses with `MailboxHandle.wait_or()`. The difference was that passing `timeout=-1` to `wait()` would cause it to block forever (even though `timeout=-0.9` or `timeout=-1.1` would cause it to timeout immediately).

Changes:

```py
wait(timeout=-1)      # Old
wait_or(timeout=None) # New

# Old:
result = wait(...)
assert result
# New:
result = wait_or(...)

# Old:
result = wait(...)
if result:
    ...
else:
    ...
# New:
try:
    result = wait_or(...)
except TimeoutError:
    ...
else:
    ...
```

refactor: show operation stats on init (#9431)

Display a message during `wandb.init()` that describes the work being done and any errors.

Before, `wandb.init()` would simply print `wandb: Waiting for wandb.init()...` with an old-style spinner.

commit message:
refactor: raise MailboxClosedError when creating handle in closed mailbox (#9465)

Raise an error instead of allowing the creation of a handle to which a response will never be delivered.

This PR also updates `StreamRecord` in `legacy-service` to own its own `Mailbox` instead of sharing one from `StreamMux`. A `StreamRecord` corresponds to a Run and starts up a `MessageRouter` that delivers responses to the mailbox. When the run ends, the `MessageRouter` closes the mailbox, so it cannot be reused by future runs.

There was no need for StreamRecords to share a Mailbox because a Record delivered to a stream can only get a Result from that same stream. Using different Mailbox instances can never result in a situation where `require_response` is called on one `Mailbox` and the result is delivered to another.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: add request ID to ServerRequest (#9474)

Add a `request_id` field to the `ServerRequest` proto that is equal to `mailbox_slot` for all `Record` requests and `Result` responses.

Without a request ID, the only way to associate responses to requests is to send one request at a time and wait for a response. This requires knowing which requests do and do not generate responses: as of now, only the ServerInformAttachRequest produces a response.

This complicates the semantics of the `SockClient` object. Only one thread can read the socket at any time, but `SockClient.read_server_response` has two callsites:

* It's called in a loop by `MessageRouter` (when using the `MessageSockRouter` subclass)
* It's invoked by `SockClient.send_and_recv`
    * This does the "send one request and wait for a response" scheme

Anytime we call `send_and_recv`, we assume there is no `MessageRouter` for that `SockClient`. Once a `MessageRouter` is created, we cannot call `send_and_recv`.

In `wandb_init.py::_attach()`, the `service.inform_attach(attach_id=attach_id)` line results in a call to `send_and_recv`, so a `MessageRouter` cannot exist at this point. Right now, a `MessageSockRouter` is created implicitly when creating an `InterfaceSock`, which is created when calling `backend.ensure_launched` later in `_attach`.

This bit me while I was trying to decouple `InterfaceShared` from `MessageRouter`. The most natural lifetime for the `MessageSockRouter` is the same as the `SockClient`. But this is created in `wandb.setup()`, which `_attach` must call before `inform_attach`. This would not have been a problem had the `Mailbox` been the only way to await responses.

fix: format specifier in WorkSentinel DebugInfo() (#9504)

Fixes the format specifier used in `WorkSentinel.DebugInfo()`. Using `%s` is incorrect when the argument (of interface type `any`) does not have the concrete type `string`. Specifically, it was producing the string

```
WorkSentinel(%!s(stream.senderSentinel=1))
```

Where `%!s` is `fmt.Sprintf`'s way of indicating that it caught and suppressed a panic. Now, with the added `String()` method on the `senderSentinel` type, the above becomes

```
WorkSentinel(senderSentinel(1))
```

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: change Mailbox to operate on ServerRequest / ServerResponse (#9488)

Generalize `Mailbox` to work on the `ServerRequest` / `ServerResponse` level instead of `Record` / `Result`.

`MailboxHandleT` is a generic class that replaces `MailboxHandle` to allow for both `MailboxHandleT[pb.Result]` and `MailboxHandleT[spb.ServerResponse]`. `MailboxHandle` is an alias to `MailboxHandleT[pb.Result]` to keep this PR small, but the next PR completes the renaming.

`Mailbox.deliver()` now requires `spb.ServerResponse` instead of `pb.Result`. The only callsite is in `MessageRouter`, which I updated. Unfortunately, `legacy-service` uses `MessageRouter` internally, so it has to continue to handle the `pb.Result` codepath. To do this, it creates an `spb.ServerResponse()` and sets its `result_communicate` to the given `pb.Result`.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: remove `_router` from `InterfaceShared` (#9469)

Separate `MessageRouter` from `InterfaceShared`. A `MessageRouter` is a handle on a thread that delivers results from the service into a `Mailbox`.

This PR also updates `inform_attach` to use `Mailbox` and removes the deprecated `SockClient.send_and_recv` mechanism. This is necessary because `send_and_recv` assumes nothing else is reading on the socket, but this PR causes a reader thread to be created earlier in `wandb_init.py::_attach()`.

There can only be one `MessageSockRouter` per socket, and there is only one socket connection to the service per client process. If `InterfaceShared` owns `MessageSockRouter`, then there can only be one `InterfaceShared` instance at a time, and therefore only a single run at a time.

This PR makes code that instantiates `InterfaceShared` be responsible for managing a `MessageRouter`. There are only three such places:

* In `Backend`, when using the `x_disable_service` setting
* In `ServiceConnection`, in normal operation
    * The `ServiceConnection` owns a socket, so it also owns the router
    * The router thread lives as long as the socket is around, until `wandb.teardown()`
* In `streams.py` in `legacy-service`
    * Each `StreamRecord`, corresponding to an active run, owns an `InterfaceQueue` and a `MessageQueueRouter`

refactor: allow multiple streams per connection in core (#9528)

Removes the `nc.stream` field and replaces it by calls to `streamMux.GetStream()`.

The risk is if we ever send messages without a stream ID to wandb-core, they will not be processed. `InterfaceSock` assigns a stream ID on all outgoing records; `ServiceConnection` in `service_connection.py` assigns a stream ID on Init, Finish, Attach and Start requests.

I have not checked other clients, but note that they would not work with legacy-service since it always requires the stream ID to be set.

commit message:
fix: default reinit to "finish_previous" in notebooks (#9569)

Adds a `"default"` option to `reinit` that behaves like `"finish_previous"` in notebooks and `"return_previous"` elsewhere.

Originally broken in 0.19.0 in https://github.com/wandb/wandb/pull/8649. The type of `reinit` used to be incorrectly annotated as `bool` but initialized to `None`. After that PR rewrote Settings using pydantic, `reinit` started to be initialized to `False` instead of `None`. Then https://github.com/wandb/wandb/pull/9445 removed the `settings._jupyter` check in `wandb_init.py` because 

```
settings.reinit or (settings._jupyter and settings.reinit is not False)
```

was equivalent to `settings.reinit` since `reinit` could not be `None`.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: support per run logging (#9540)

Defines the `wb_logging` module to filter out log messages for other runs from a run's log file.

Since most of our log statements don't include a run ID, to support multiple simultaneous active runs we need to direct only relevant log messages to each run's `debug.log` file. Without this PR, all log messages go to all runs' log files. With this PR, log messages that are known to be irrelevant to a run (due to `wb_logging.log_to_run(...)` being used for another run ID) are filtered out.

Messages logged outside the context of `wb_logging.log_to_run` are written to all runs' log files with a `[no run ID]` prefix. This can happen if we forget to use `wb_logging.log_to_run()` somewhere, or if a message really is not run-specific.

This only affects logging handlers added through `wb_logging.add_file_handler()`, so it does not affect log messages from `legacy-service` which go to `debug-internal.log` or those from the CLI. I am not sure where messages from the public API go; I think we do not store them?

NOTE: There is old code that uses logging to output to the console, which was always wrong but worked on occasion. I found one instance of this in our Jupyter code and fixed all messages that look like they should be user-facing, but I don't have a way to find all instances.

commit message:
chore: attempt to fix test_asyncio_compat_run flake (#9660)

Prints timestamps in the test for future debugging, and protects access to `_got_cancelled` with a lock to ensure it is synchronized.

The test [fails on rare occasion](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/wandb/wandb/45473/workflows/f02fd269-1721-4922-931f-b199d06e2d1c/jobs/1363571/tests) with the message `FAIL: Interrupted but not cancelled`. Since the `__exit__` of the `ThreadPoolExecutor` used by `asyncio_compat.run` blocks until the future completes, there are only two ways this can happen:

1. The KeyboardInterrupt is really not received by the main thread and the asyncio task is not cancelled
2. The asyncio task is cancelled, but the main thread does not observe the new value of `_got_cancelled`

If the problem is (2), the lock will fix it. If the problem is (1), the timestamps will make that clear.

---

Note that [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/a/53780395) suggests that (2) isn't possible in Python, but this could be implementation dependent ([PEP 583](https://peps.python.org/pep-0583) attempted to state some guarantees but was withdrawn). In other languages, it can happen if the two threads run on different CPUs, and the new value of the variable is stored in a CPU cache. We use Cython in CI so all threads should run on the same CPU, but maybe there's some other race that I'm not seeing.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: improve run decorator types (#9653)

Improves run decorator types so that Pylance can correctly infer decorated method arguments and return values.

I'm not sure if it is a recent Pylance change, but annotating a decorator as returning a `Callable` (with no parameters) causes Pylance to treat a method's return type as `Any`. For example, VSCode fails to find the reference to `Artifact.download()` in `Run.use_model()` because of this!

This PR also removes the unnecessary `_run_decorator` wrapper class, renames decorators, adds documentation, and cleans up implementations. I also removed the `only_warn` parameter from `_raise_if_finished` (formerly `_noop_on_finish`), which was only used by `_console_raw_callback`. This is OK because `StreamRawWrapper` catches exceptions.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: improve types and docs in jupyter.py (#9662)

Improves types in `jupyter.py` and the usage of `Notebook` in `wandb_init.py`. Since `wandb_init.py` is the only place where `Notebook` is used, it's safe to add a `run` parameter to `save_history` to avoid using the global run.

The silly `if TYPE_CHECKING: import wandb.jupyter` in `wandb_init.py` is needed because of our terrible lazy-loading system. Importing it directly causes `test_notebooks.py` to fail because monkeypatching stops working (even though `test_notebooks.py` never uses the functionality in `wandb_init.py`). The entire problem can be solved by removing the `jupyter = _lazyloader.LazyLoader(...)` line from `wandb/__init__.py`, but that would be a breaking change.

commit message:
refactor: do not raise in Artifact.download() if an offline run exists (#9695)

## Description

Removes the `util._is_offline()` check in `Artifact.download()` which relies on a global `wandb.run`.

This check was originally added in PR #8009 because of a crash in wandb-core, but the crash no longer happens.

## Testing

The repro in the PR that added the check can be used:

```python
# artifact_download_offline.py
import os

import wandb

os.environ["WANDB_MODE"] = "offline"
os.environ["WANDB_DEBUG"] = "true"


def download_artifact(artifact_name: str):
    artifact = wandb.Api().artifact(artifact_name)
    return artifact.download(root="/tmp/wandb_artifacts")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # TODO: Set these to any existing run.
    run_path = "wandb/timoffex-test/r0sczcuf"
    project = "timoffex-test"

    # TODO: Set this to any existing artifact.
    artifact_name = "wandb/timoffex-test/trained-model:v2"

    with wandb.init(project=project) as run:
        run.restore(name="output.log", replace=True, run_path=run_path)

    artifact_path = download_artifact(artifact_name)
    print(f"Artifact downloaded to: {artifact_path}")
```

From this PR, the following uses core and works fine:

```
python artifact_download_offline.py
```

From 0.17.5 (the version at the time of the PR), the following stalls:

```
WANDB__REQUIRE_CORE=true python artifact_download_offline.py
```

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: remove the workspace option to wandb ipython magic (#9709)

Removes the `-w` / `--workspace` option to the `wandb` cell/line IPython magic because it is a no-op.

I attempted fixing it as well, but it does not appear to work: using `%%wandb -w` in a cell that initializes a run produces an iframe that fails to load.

The original code:

```python
if self.opts.get("workspace", False):
    if self.path is None and wandb.run:
        self.path = wandb.run.path
if isinstance(self.path, str):
    object = self.api.from_path(self.path)
else:
    object = wandb.run
if object is None:
    if wandb.Api().api_key is None:
        return "You must be logged in to render wandb in jupyter, run `wandb.login()`"
    else:
        object = self.api.project(...)
return object.to_html(self.height, hidden=False)
```

If `workspace` is False:

* If `self.path` is set (`%%wandb entity/project/id`), it is used
* Else, if `wandb.run` is set, it is used

If `workspace` is True:

* If `self.path` is set, it is used
* Else, if `wandb.run` is set, its path is used
    * `wandb.run.path` always has 3 components, so `api.from_path()` returns a `public.Run`
    * `public.Run.to_html` is identical to `wandb.run.to_html`

So `workspace` did not have any effect.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: avoid global run in wandb ipython magic (#9710)

Refactors the wandb IPython magic (`%%wandb` / `%wandb`) to avoid using the global run when displaying a run as part of `wandb.init()`.

The old `maybe_display()` function was only called when printing the Run header when initializing a run, but it used `wandb.run` to decide what to display. Now it accepts a run explicitly.

`wandb.run` is still used when running the `%wandb` magic on its own, like

```python
# --- Cell 1 ---
run = wandb.init()

# --- Cell 2 ---
# This creates an iframe displaying the above run's page.
%wandb -h 600
```

On the other hand, this uses the explicit run and will continue to work when `wandb.run` is removed:

```python
%%wandb -h 600
with wandb.init() as run:
    ...
```

refactor: don't use global run in printer.py (#9716)

Instead of checking whether `wandb.run` has `silent` set to True in its settings, use the global settings. This matches the behavior for terminal output which relies on `termsetup()` whose `_silent` parameter can only come from an explicit `silent` setting passed to `wandb.setup()`.

commit message:
refactor: clean up deprecate.py (#9717)

* Improves wording in the docstring

    * The only places it's available and not passed were in `wandb_run.py`

Instead of printing a message when the user is on `wandb-core`, which has been the norm for a long time now, print a warning on init when the user is on `legacy-service`.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
feat: reinit="create_new" setting for multiple simultaneous runs in one process (#9746)

DUPLICATED FROM PR #9562 which I accidentally merged into the wrong branch.

* WB-23108, WB-24208
* Docs: https://github.com/wandb/docs/pull/1145

Adds a `create_new` option to the `reinit` setting which causes `wandb.init()` to create a new run even if other runs exist. This should eventually become the default, and the other options ("return_previous" and "finish_previous") should be deprecated.

Although it's possible to pass `reinit` as a `wandb.init()` argument, the best way to use this is with `wandb.setup()`.

Here is an example that uses the `create_new` setting to (serially) run multiple sub-experiments while logging their results to another run:

```python
wandb.setup(wandb.Settings(reinit="create_new"))

with wandb.init() as experiment_results_run:
    for ...:
        with wandb.init() as run:
            # The do_experiment() function logs fine-grained metrics
            # to the given run and then returns result metrics that
            # we'd like to track separately.
            experiment_results = do_experiment(run)

            # After each experiment, we log its results to a parent
            # run. Each point in the parent run's charts corresponds
            # to one experiment's results.
            experiment_results_run.log(experiment_results)
```

---

This PR also removes `util._is_offline()` and replaces it with a heuristic that uses the newly added `most_recent_active_run`. This way, `_is_offline` continues to work as expected in most cases.

commit message:
refactor: rewrite RunParams and clean up fork/rewind/resume.go (#9791)

Cleans up `internal/runbranch` in wandb-core to prepare for an UpsertBucket-related refactor:

* Simplified `RunParams` and organized it for better readability
* Changed fork/rewind/resume.go to modify the `RunParams` in-place instead of returning updates that are then merged
* Instead of accepting `RunParams` and `RunPath`, fork/rewind/resume.go read the entity/project/run ID from `RunParams`. The `RunPath` parameter was always derived from `RunParams` in `Sender`.
* Removed the `Config` field of `RunParams` and made rewind/resume.go accept and mutate a `RunConfig` directly

In the `Sender`, `startState` now starts out as `nil` and becomes set when processing the first `RunRecord` (if an error occurs, it is set back to `nil`).

`Sender` no longer clones the `RunRecord` at the start of `sendRun`: it is cloned immediately before it is mutated (by merging `startState.Proto()` into it) wherever that happens.

commit message:
refactor: create internal/runmetadata (#9814)

Creates `internal/runmetadata` and fills it out with unimplemented methods to serve as an easy-to-review base for later PRs that implement it in parts.

`RunMetadata` will contain the majority of the implementation.

`RunUpdateWork` is the glue that makes `Handler` and `Sender` interact with `RunMetadata`. The `RunMetadata` object will live on a `Stream`, and `Stream` will turn `RunRecord` into `RunUpdateWork`. Its `Accept()` method returns `true`, corresponding to `Handler` unconditionally forwarding the record; `Process()` is the `Sender` portion. `BypassOfflineMode()` returns true corresponding to `Handler` setting `AlwaysSend` on the `RunRecord`.

I only updated files that have a conditional import. There are many other files where we import from `typing` where we could import from `typing_extensions`, but updating them manually just for the sake of consistency doesn't seem worth it.

commit message:
feat: support cloud files for TB sync using wandb-core (#9849)

Fixes WB-21735. Documentation PR: https://github.com/wandb/docs/pull/1338

Replaces paths in `internal/tensorboard` with a new `LocalOrCloudPath` type. This requires some additional work when guessing root directories, so that's moved out of `tensorboard.go` into a new `rootdirguesser.go` file.

## Cloud support

GCS format: `gs://bucket/path/to/file`. GCS uses the standard Google Cloud [application default credentials](https://pkg.go.dev/gocloud.dev@v0.41.0/blob/gcsblob#hdr-URLs), which can be configured using `gcloud auth application-default login`.

S3 format: `s3://bucket/path/to/file`. S3 uses its standard [default credentials](https://pkg.go.dev/gocloud.dev@v0.41.0/blob/s3blob#hdr-URLs). The credentials file can be configured using `aws configure`, but environment variables might also work. I'm not sure how to use IAM instead of access keys and whether this is possible with the Go SDK, so there may be limitations (which are likely also present in TensorFlow's built-in support).

Azure format: `az://account/container/path/to/file`. Azure uses credentials set by `az login`, but also requires the environment variables `AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT` and `AZURE_STORAGE_KEY` to be set. These variables and some alternatives are described [here](https://pkg.go.dev/gocloud.dev@v0.41.0/blob/azureblob#hdr-URLs). In contrast, TensorFlow's Azure support requires the `TF_AZURE_STORAGE_KEY` variable to be set. So to run a script that uses TensorFlow and W&B with Azure log directories, one must use a pattern like

```sh
AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT=myaccount \
AZURE_STORAGE_KEY=mykey \
TF_AZURE_STORAGE_KEY="$AZURE_STORAGE_KEY" \
python my_script.py
```

## Testing

The only code that's specific to different clouds is in `localorcloudpath.go`; all other code uses the generic API provided by gocloud.dev, even for local files.

For manually testing, create a bucket in any of the supported clouds and then use this script:

Script:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
import wandb

# This import is required for its side-effect of enabling
# cloud paths for tf.summary.create_file_writer().
# It's not necessary for GCS.
import tensorflow_io


with wandb.init(sync_tensorboard=True) as run:
    path = # s3:// or gs:// URL here
    with tf.summary.create_file_writer(path).as_default():
        tf.summary.scalar("x", 0.3, step=1)
        tf.summary.scalar("y", 0.7, step=1)
        tf.summary.scalar("z", 2.1, step=1)

        tf.summary.scalar("x", 0.5, step=2)
        tf.summary.scalar("x", 0.9, step=3)

        tf.summary.scalar("y", 1.1, step=2)
        tf.summary.scalar("z", 3.5, step=2)
        tf.summary.scalar("y", 0.8, step=3)
```

Confirmed this works with GCS, S3 and Azure (though for S3, my script ended with a segfault after the run finished, which I think must have come from TensorFlow itself).

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: don't require legacy-service in CLI (#9912)

Removes `wandb.require("legacy-service")` in `cli.py` and uses `wandb_setup._setup(settings=..., start_service=False)` instead of `wandb.setup(settings=...)` to modify global settings.

This was causing an erroneous warning

> wandb: WARNING Using legacy-service, which is deprecated. If this is unintentional, you can fix it by ensuring you do not call `wandb.require('legacy-service')` and do not set the WANDB_X_REQUIRE_LEGACY_SERVICE environment variable.

The `require` was originally added out of caution in case any users were running on machines that didn't support `wandb-core` before making it the default. If `wandb.require("legacy-service")` isn't used and `wandb-core` isn't supported, then `wandb.setup()` fails when trying to start up the service process. In a normal script, a user is expected to add the `require` to their code; but in the CLI, there would have been no workaround.

In `cli.py` and the login code, `wandb.setup()` is only used for global settings, and the service process isn't needed. The internal `wandb_setup._setup(start_service=False)` function was added a couple months ago for this purpose during a refactor of `wandb.init()`.

In general, we should not call `wandb.setup()` from within the SDK. After this PR, the only remaining call is in `wandb/cli/beta.py` which seems valid, and two innocuous ones in `wandb/sdk/artifacts/artifact.py` and `wandb/sdk/wandb_init.py` which I will remove separately.


## Testing

Use `pip install -e <wandb>`, then delete `wandb/bin/wandb-core` and attempt to use the CLI:

* `wandb login`
* `wandb projects` is good enough to test the `_get_cling_api()` path

commit message:
refactor: enable and fix TRY400 (logger.exception() instead of logger.error()) (#9906)

https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/error-instead-of-exception/

All fixes are manual because in most cases I had to remove redundant string-interpolation of the error. In a few spots, `logger.exception()` would have been called multiple times in a row, so I condensed those into a single `logger.exception()` call. Also, in `internal_api.py`, I simplified some `logger.exception()` calls to not parse the underlying error; I am assuming all the needed info will appear in log files when the exception is formatted.

I think some of the stranger `logger.error()` invocations came from a time when we didn't consistently set up the `wandb` logger, causing their messages to sometimes get printed to the user's console. That's probably why `cli.py` had statements like `logger.error("=== %s ===", e)`.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: fix a few instances of TRY300 (#9918)

https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/try-consider-else/

This one takes some manual work to really fix, and I don't enable this lint in this PR because its suggestion can be a little misleading. For instance, it will produce a diagnostic on this:

```python
try:
    result = computation()
    return result
except SomeError:
    return other
```

The lint message will make it seem that the solution is this:

```python
try:
    result = computation()
except SomeError:
    return other
else:
    return result
```

But an even better solution is

```python
try:
    return computation()
except SomeError:
    return other
```

In many cases in our codebase, the right fix is to narrow the scope of the `try-except` rather than to use `try-except-else`. It also sometimes makes sense to not use an `else` block at all, especially when the exception handler is an early return.

commit message:
refactor: use runupserter, delete old Sender code (#9804)

Replaces all old UpsertBucket code with `internal/runupserter`.

`RunUpserter` lives on a `Stream` and is operated on by `RunUpdateWork` in the sender goroutine. `Handler` and `Sender` no longer receive `RunRecord` and the corresponding code has been removed---when we implement syncing in wandb-core, we will create `RunUpdateWork` from `RunRecord` values the same way it happens in the `Stream` in this PR.

Unlike the old code in `Sender`, `RunUpserter` can batch updates to run parameters (such as its notes and tags) with updates to the run config in a single upload. Also, the updates happen asynchronously and do not block the `Sender` from doing other work.

commit message:
refactor: enable and fix TRY300 (try-consider-else) (#9923)

https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/try-consider-else/

The lint is a little misleading: it's not about preferring an `else` clause in `try-except` blocks, but about narrowing the scope of a `try-except`. So, for instance:

```python
try:
    result = do_something()
    do_something_else()
    return result
except DoSomethingError:
    return something_else
```

should really be written as

```python
try:
    result = do_something()
except DoSomethingError:
    return something_else

do_something_else()
return result
```

An `else` clause would be appropriate if the `except DoSomethingError` clause didn't return, or if it helps with readability by improving vertical alignment or flow of logic.

I fixed a few cases, and added ignores for the remaining violations. This at least prevents this kind of code in new files.

commit message:
fix: restore original image normalization behavior (#9982)

For comparison, the original code is [here](https://github.com/wandb/wandb/blob/fa9063d08d753434676e1cbe3206932faf839f23/wandb/sdk/data_types/image.py#L525-L533).

```python
        dmin = np.min(data)
        if dmin < 0:
            data = (data - np.min(data)) / np.ptp(data)
        if np.max(data) <= 1.0:
            data = (data * 255).astype(np.int32)

        return data.clip(0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
```

Note that this rescales [-1, 1] images to the _entire_ [0, 255] range mapping the image's minimum to 0 and its maximum to 255. For [0, 1] images, this simply multiplies them by 255.

After a refactor, PR #9883 changed the code to something almost similar, but with a bug:

```python
    if np.min(data) < 0:
        data = data - np.min(data)

    if np.ptp(data) != 0:
        data = data / np.ptp(data)

    if np.max(data) <= 1.0:
        data = (255 * data).astype(np.int32)

    return data.clip(0, 255)
```

For [0, 1] images this is broken: the first if statement gets skipped, but the second if statement usually matches. Take a grayscale 1x2 image `[[0.5, 0.6]]`: its `np.ptp` (peak-to-peak) value is 0.1, so dividing by it produces `[[5, 6]]` which is then returned, but the image's correct [0, 255] form is `[[127, 153]]`.

This PR restores the behavior for [0, 255] and [0, 1] images. I also took the liberty of changing the [-1, 1] behavior slightly: instead of mapping [min, max] to [0, 255], I map [-1, 1] to [0, 255]. I think this might have been the original intention; otherwise, images like `[[-0.1, 0.1]]` and `[[-0.8, 0.8]]` were both being converted to `[[0, 255]]`.

```python
import numpy as np
import wandb

x = np.array([[0.68235186, 0.05382102],[0.22035987, 0.18437181]])
print(wandb.Image(x).to_data_array())
```

In wandb==0.20.0, this prints `[[1, 0], [0, 0]]`. With this PR, it correctly prints `[[173, 13], [56, 47]]`.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix: calling method on None in printer.py (#10009)

MyPy doesn't catch this because `display()` is untyped, but PyRight notes that it can return `None` in this part of its implementation:

```python
    if not InteractiveShell.initialized():
        # Directly print objects.
        print(*objs)
        return
```

I don't think this happens for us (so I doubt any user hit this), but the code was wrong since its logic is meant to handle `None`.

I also:

* swapped the order of `@property` and `@override` to satisfy PyRight (the result of `@property` is not `Callable`, but `@override`'s type technically requires its argument to be `Callable`)
* updated the name of the unused argument in `progress_close` to match the method it's overriding (since technically it can be passed by name)

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: wandb-core entrypoint code (#9989)

Slight clean-up of `server.go` and `main.go`.

In `server.go`:

* Don't do work in the `Server` constructor (`NewServer()`)
* Put `ServerParams` near `NewServer()` to make the function signature easier to see
* Extract port-file logic to its own file
    * I removed the `f.Sync()` step because we do not need it, and having to ask myself "why is it here" each time I see it wastes time. In fact, we can almost go without even closing the file because the client will not interpret it until "EOF" is written---so the only way for this to break is if the OS could somehow write the last three bytes of the file before the rest of it.

      As far as I understand, the purpose of `fsync` before a rename is for crash resilience. If no crash happens, then reads of a file after it is closed will return its updated contents because the OS has them in memory. If a crash happens and the rename completed but the file contents weren't written to disk yet, you could see partial content. But we don't need the port file after a crash.

In `main.go`:

* Break implementation out into a function that returns an exit code, and call `os.Exit()` in `main()`

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: use Unix domain sockets to connect to wandb-core (#9995)

Fixes WB-25232, WB-25245, WB-25138.

Makes `wandb-core` listen on a Unix domain socket if possible and fall back to a localhost socket if not.

~After confirming that Unix domain sockets work in all environments we support, we should drop the localhost fallback as it could be a security issue (or check the peer's UID and refuse connections from mismatched UIDs)~ (UPDATE: Python on Windows does not support Unix sockets, so localhost sockets will remain). The reason is that it bypasses the permission model, letting processes running as different users send messages to the server. This creates a potential pathway for such processes to affect the user's script. This is probably why connections to localhost sockets are blocked in some Databricks environments.

Unix domain sockets should work on Linux, macOS ~and updated Windows versions (after \~2017)~ (they work on Windows, but not supported in Python). Reasons this code could fail include:

* If we don't have read/write permissions for `os.TempDir()` or `/tmp`
* If the socket's path is too long (apparently, on some systems the limit [may be 92 bytes](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/unix.7.html))
    * On my macOS, the `os.TempDir()` is "/var/folders/v0/mtcq4gwj13q7lzyj4fsq5hz40000gp/T/", resulting in an 85-character path
    * The fallback to `/tmp` on Unix-like systems should help

commit message:
fix: potential race conditions in Sender on exit (#10041)

Fixes potential race conditions in `Sender.finishRunSync()` by ensuring any objects not guarded by `Sender.mu` are concurrency-aware. The main problem is with `Finish()` methods, which often involve a `WaitGroup.Wait()` call. Calling `Wait()` and `Add()` simultaneously can cause a panic.

These race conditions can only occur if certain kinds of records are processed after `Exit`. I think there is a race condition in the Python client that can allow it to sometimes send `OutputRaw` records after `Exit`.

Fixes a race condition where the client may send `OutputRaw` records after an `Exit` record, despite `wandb_run.py` unregistering `console_capture.py` callbacks before calling `deliver_exit()`. author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix: clear console capture callbacks on error (#10071)

Makes `console_capture.py` clear all callbacks if a callback raises an error.

Since callbacks are invoked when stdout or stderr is being written to, and since errors are likely to be printed to the console, this can trigger an infinite loop. This is especially problematic for `KeyboardInterrupt` as it makes it difficult to stop the program using Ctrl+C if a callback is permanently stuck (imagine a callback that does `time.sleep(600)`).

Also updates `console_capture.py` to log and suppress regular Exceptions thrown by callbacks, since these will almost always be W&B bugs that shouldn't propagate to the user's `print()` statements.

perf: optimize artifact download by adding fast size check before MD5 computation

- Reduces artifact download time from ~4 minutes to ~0.1 seconds for 100K files
- Maintains backward compatibility with MD5 fallback for corrupted files
- Fixes performance issue where already-downloaded artifacts take too long to verify

hashes for all files, even when files were already correctly downloaded.

commit message:
fix: flaky test in test_keras.py (#10161)

Makes `test_keras.py` use the subprocess module instead of `runpy` to fix a flaky test.

Example of a flake: https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/wandb/wandb/49366/workflows/55c71ca7-bb87-4b4b-b022-1aa2dfca8626/jobs/1427172/tests

The flake was likely happening because of a race condition: `execute_script` would return after all `run.summary[...] = ...` statements in `WandbCallback` were executed but not necessarily processed by `wandb-core`. By executing the script using `subprocess`, it triggers `wandb.teardown()` at the end and blocks until `wandb-core` finishes all of its work.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: expose `wandb.Run` (#10175)

We have it defined in `__init__.pyi` but not in `__init__.py`.

I updated a lot of code to use `wandb.Run` instead of `wandb.wandb_sdk.wandb_run.Run`, but there are still some spots left (like the many `LocalRun` definitions in `data_types`).

## Safety

The line

```python
# wandb/__init__.py
from wandb import sdk as wandb_sdk
```

triggers the line

```python
# wandb/sdk/__init__.py
from .wandb_run import finish
```

which executes `wandb/sdk/wandb_run.py`. So the new line,

```python
# wandb/__init__.py
from wandb.sdk.wandb_run import Run
```

does not perform an import, and its addition cannot introduce any new import cycles or change the import behavior in any way.

commit message:
chore: improve test_metaflow.py runtimes (#10200)

Speeds up `test_metaflow.py` by:

* (biggest improvement) Adding `wandb.setup()`: each Metaflow step runs in a subprocess, and it takes some time to start `wandb-core`, connect to it, and then shut it down each time
* (surprisingly tiny improvement, maybe even negligible) Simplifying the models and reducing the amount of training data

The tests are still quite slow, with the biggest slowdown being that `wandb.init()` requires logging in which adds ~3s to each step. Another factor is that `@wandb_log` uploads each step's outputs as artifacts, which ends up being slow even with pretty small artifacts (0.5s-1.0s).

Timing changes (comparing this PR to main):

| test | before | after |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| test_flow_pytorch | 177s | 132s |
| test_flow_decostep | 119s | 95s |
| test_flow_foreach | 119s | 99s |
| test_flow_decoclass | 110s | 85s |
| test_flow_decoboth | 97s | 83s |

Total improvement is ~128s but it's split between 4 parallel workers (=> 30s). But the tests should use less CPU, which might allow other tests to run faster.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: rethink where TensorBoard lives (#10039)

Moves TensorBoard awareness to an earlier stage in wandb-core: the `work.Schedule()` method, which happens before `Accept()` (Handler) and `Process()` (Sender).

## Motivation

This is motivated by the TensorBoard integration creating the last remaining case where the Sender must send messages back to the Handler: on receiving an Exit record, the Sender waits to shut down TensorBoard because it may generate additional records. This PR allows completely getting rid of this mechanism, replacing `Sentinel()` by `Schedule()`. The next PR does this refactor.

## Design notes

The design reasoning for this PR is that the simplest way to treat the TensorBoard integration is to pretend the client is directly calling run methods (`run.log()`, `run.save()`). If this were true, then the client would shut down TensorBoard before sending an Exit record; we simulate this at `Schedule()` time to maintain the illusion.

There's a nuance that will be important later: `Schedule()` can reorder records. For an online run this is OK, since `Schedule()` runs before the Handler when records may be reordered; but during `wandb sync` (not yet implemented in wandb-core), this is problematic because `Schedule()` is given records that have already been written. That's a problem because of flow control (also not yet implemented), for which the simplest implementation assumes records arrive in the same order they appear in the transaction log. The `WaitGroup` parameter to `Schedule()` is the solution: `sync` will `Wait()` on it to prevent reordering.

refactor: no plum-dispatch in metaflow integration (#10202)

commit message:
refactor: no more Work.Sentinel() (#10040)

Removes `Work.Sentinel()` because it is not needed as of PR #10039.

`Work.Sentinel()` is a renaming of what used to be called `DeferRequest`. The Sender uses it to flush the Record pipeline (Handler -> Sender) after shutting down subcomponents. In the past, it was common to generate new records while processing an `Exit` record: after calling a subcomponent's `Finish()` method, the Sender would use a Sentinel (formerly DeferRequest) to ensure it processed any new records before shutting down later components. All such instances have been removed now: nothing in `Sender.finishRunSync()` can generate additional records:

* `consoleLogsSender.Finish()` communicates directly with `runfiles.Uploader` and `FileStream` 
* `streamSummary()` directly calls `FileStream`
* `uploadSummaryFile()` and `uploadConfigFile()` directly call `runfiles.Uploader`
* No records are generated while waiting for `artifactWG.Wait()`
    * See the only two places where `Add()` is called
    * Note that no calls to `ExtraWork.AddWork()` appear in artifact code
* Likewise for `sendJobFlush()` (it uploads an artifact)
* `fileWatcher.Finish()` emits events that are used only by `runfiles.Uploader`, which does not generate records
* `runfilesUploader.UploadRemaining()`, `runfilesUploader.Finish()` and `fileTransferManager.Close()` are all safe
* `finishFileStream()` just calls into `FileStream`

The last remaining obstacle to dropping this mechanism was the TensorBoard integration, which PR #10039 refactors.

## Sync considerations

Some old versions of `wandb` (I don't remember which) incorrectly write records after `Exit`. The original code would have sometimes processed these and sometimes not, depending on how fast the transaction log was read. This PR will log an error and ignore such records.

Since we don't implement `wandb sync` using wandb-core yet, this PR is safe. When adding `wandb sync` later, we will want to account for these transaction logs. Note that `sync.py` already does this to some degree, and we'll need to carry that over anyway.

commit message:
refactor: write to transaction log synchronously (#10060)

Refactors `writer.go` to finish writing records to the transaction log before forwarding them.

This is the original behavior, which we changed because it was unnecessary. It will soon become necessary for "flow control": if we discard Work because the Sender is blocked and then try to read it from the transaction log when it's unblocked, the Work needs to have been fully written.

One of our motivations before was to avoid blocking on the transaction log if writing to disk is slow---but note that blocking would have happened anyway once the finite storeChan buffer filled up.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: fix SeekRecord to allow seeking in the transaction log (#10141)

Makes Store's Reader's `SeekRecord` method work correctly with our customizations to the LevelDB file format, so that it can be used for flow control.

The comment at the top of `record.go` has a good description of the format, but the gist of it is that the stream of data (i.e. the transaction log file) is divided into 32 KiB blocks. The fixed block size makes it possible to read data even if a block is corrupted (skipping any records that had some data in that block).

Our customization keeps the 32 KiB block boundaries, but writes a custom header into the first 7 bytes of the stream. This causes the first block to start at byte 7 and to contain at most (32 * 1024 - 7) bytes. This is regrettable because we could have just put the header into its own LevelDB record keeping the format unchanged.

This PR makes `record.go` aware of the W&B header, replacing the `initialData` Writer parameter and `ReadHeader` Reader method. I decided against extending those abstractions (like by adding a `initialHeaderLength` field to `Reader`) because we only use `record.go` for the transaction log anyway, and mentioning the W&B header explicitly makes the reason for the customization clear. Either way would have worked though.

commit message:
refactor: create Factory structs for Handler, Writer, Sender (#10278)

Creates `HandlerFactory`, `WriterFactory` and `SenderFactory` structs to be used instead of directly injecting `Handler`, `Writer` and `Sender`.

These allow separating injectable values from explicit parameters. `WriterFactory.New` is an example: the `fwdChan` is an explicit parameter, whereas `Logger` and `Settings` are provided implicitly through injection.

`wire` simplifies construction but in doing so hides object lifecycles and ownership. Objects with lifecycles (like `RunWork`, `TBHandler`, `FileStream`, etc.) are best constructed explicitly; shared objects without lifecycles (`observability.CoreLogger`, `Settings`, etc.) can continue to be injected.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: featurechecker context parameter (#10285)

Makes `Context` a function parameter rather than a struct field in `ServerFeaturesCache` so that each caller can provide its own context.

There's one `ServerFeaturesCache` per `Stream`, but `context.Background()` is the only reasonable context at that level. Right now we use `ExtraWork.BeforeRunEndCtx()`, but that should be passed by callers directly to `GetFeature()` instead. The `BeforeRunEndCtx` will soon not be injectable because `RunWork` needs lifecycle management and should be explicitly constructed.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
chore: fix coverage collection for tests that run subprocesses (#10347)

Best demonstrated with an example:

```bash
nox -s 'functional_tests-3.10' -- tests/system_tests/test_functional/asyncio_compat_run/test_asyncio_compat_run.py
coverage report --include=wandb/sdk/lib/asyncio_compat.py

# Output before this change:
#   wandb/sdk/lib/asyncio_compat.py      85     61    28%
# Output after this change:
#   wandb/sdk/lib/asyncio_compat.py      85     26    69%
```

The `--cov` option expects a value (it's not just a switch) in all documentation, so we appear to have been misusing it. **Why** does that break coverage in this way? I couldn't tell you. But I think it has to do with paths because I get the same 28% in a fresh venv doing this:

```bash
uv venv .venv-cov-bad
source .venv-cov-bad/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements_dev.txt
pytest --cov-report= --cov --no-cov-on-fail tests/system_tests/test_functional/asyncio_compat_run/test_asyncio_compat_run.py
```

but it becomes 69% if I make sure to use an editable install before the pytest command:

```bash
uv pip install -e .
```

commit message:
refactor: make wandb_setup.singleton() not load settings (#10361)

Changes `wandb_setup.singleton()` to not load settings from the environment and replaces `singleton_if_setup()` by a `settings_if_loaded` property.

Before this PR, `singleton_if_setup()` was used to avoid initializing settings if they weren't already initialized, mainly because tests rely on modifying environment variables in fixtures and we don't want to accidentally initialize settings before the fixtures run.

I'm adding an asyncio thread to the singleton, and `singleton()` must be used to get it because there's no alternative if `singleton_if_setup()` returns `None`. This PR prevents `singleton()` from initializing settings.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: create AsyncioManager (#10334)

Creates `AsyncioManager` to allow running `asyncio` in a separate thread and adding tasks to it.

`wandb` currently creates a new `asyncio` thread each time it waits on a mailbox handle, while a separate thread continuously polls a socket and pushes responses to the handles. This is only slightly inefficient (`wandb` programs don't need to wait mailbox handles often), so the main issue is multithreaded use of a socket. The read thread flips the socket between blocking and timeout modes; the write thread is written to work with either, but this is not robust: we've seen it throw a `BlockingIOError` which shouldn't be possible and indicates a potential race.

With `AsyncioManager`, a single long-lived `asyncio` thread will be able to run a socket reading task, occasional socket writing tasks, and mailbox tasks.

PR simplifies the `Artifact` class by removing the unnecessary private attribute `Artifact._storage_policy`.  It can still be accessed via `Artifact.manifest.storage_policy`.

Because this change doesn't alter the (formally) public API, it need not be considered a breaking change.

### Context:

- The **private** attribute `Artifact._storage_policy` is redundant with the **public** attribute `Artifact.manifest.storage_policy`, which also muddles the source of truth when determining "this artifact's storage policy".
- We notably have test code that accesses the private attribute  (`Artifact._storage_policy`) from **outside** of the `Artifact` class.
  - While occasionally justified, this is usually a pattern we should try to avoid.  It's a code smell and can often suggest underlying issues with the current design of one or more parts of the API (eg insufficient separation of concerns between classes, or something else).
  - In this case, the `storage_policy` can already be accessed via the non-private namespace `artifact.manifest.storage_policy`.
- FWIW Ruff has a linting rule for this, though we don't currently check it, as it would currently fail on too many other parts of the code: https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/private-member-access/

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: completely replace SockClient and MessageRouter (#10355)

Completely rewrites the socket code used to communicate between the Python client and wandb-core.

The main addition is ServiceClient, and there are many simplifications in Mailbox because all the async operations now happen in a single thread.

The ancient SockClient and MessageRouter classes are replaced by the much smaller and simpler ServiceClient. Instead of using multithreading, all socket communication happens in the asyncio thread. SockClient had a race condition because it flipped the socket between timeout and blocking mode in an unsynchronized way; this is no longer a problem.

commit message:
fix(artifacts): avoid extra GQL requests on linking an artifact (#10393)

Description
-----------
<!--
Include reference to internal ticket "Fixes WB-NNNNN" and/or GitHub issue "Fixes #NNNN" (if applicable)
-->
- Fixes https://wandb.atlassian.net/browse/WB-27167

When calling `artifact.link()` or `run.link_artifact()`, the current implementation makes **multiple extra GraphQL calls after the actual linking mutation**:
- 1 query to fetch the user's `default_entity` (if needed)
- 1 introspection query to check if `Organization.orgEntity` is a supported field
- 1 query to fetch the `organization` and `orgEntity`
- 1 query to check if `ServerFeatures.PROJECT_ARTIFACT_COLLECTION_MEMBERSHIP` is supported
- 1 query to finally fetch the artifact

(this is all in addition to the overhead of instantiating new `Api()` and `InternalApi()` objects within different methods.)

On newer servers, the `linkArtifact` mutation has been updated so that it returns the linked artifact membership directly.

PR updates `artifact.link()` to bypass the extra GQL requests that would previously be required **after** the link operation (by `api._artifact()`), as long as the backend server supports it.

commit message:
chore: add weave integration file (#10403)

Adds a new module `wandb.integration.weave` that exposes a stable interface `weave` can rely on to interact with `wandb`. Not meant for packages other than `weave`.

Also makes a few functions in `wandb_setup.py`​ thread-safe:

- setup(), singleton() and teardown() share a lock, so their invocations always happen in order
- most_recent_active_run(), add_active_run() and remove_active_run() share a lock as well
- finish_all_active_runs() can be called simultaneously with the other `active_run`​ methods but only from one thread at a time (so `wandb.init()`​ is still not thread-safe)
    - This is because `run.finish()`​ is not thread-safe

This way we don’t need to worry if a Run is active in a different thread from `weave.init()`​.

commit message:
refactor: server request protos for wandb beta sync (#10399)

Adds protos that will be used for communication in `wandb beta sync`. There are three requests:

- `init_sync` generates an ID for the operation, used in the other two requests
- `sync` initiates syncing and responds when done
- `sync_status` polls for status messages

This could be simpler if we had a mechanism to stream multiple responses for a request, in which case a single request could receive zero or more status updates followed by a final update. That's something we can add in the future.

commit message:
refactor: remove inform_start request (#10449)

Removes it because it has no effect other than to cause confusion.

This was sent by `wandb.init()` after a `Run` record and before a `RunStart` request.

The first thing that `wandb-core` did in response was overwrite the `Stream.settings` field which was too late anyway: everything is initialized by this time to use the first Settings object created using the settings passed to `inform_init`. Even if that worked, the settings don't change between `inform_init` and `inform_start`.

The other thing was to update the "run_url" tag on the Stream's Sentry instance, but again, this is already initialized correctly when the `observability.CoreLogger` is constructed during `inform_init` (see `internal/stream/streamlogger.go::streamLogger`).

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: call Printer.progress_close() correctly and remove text param (#10419)

I think the `text` parameter was a remnant of how we used to display `run.finish()`. The fact that this would print an empty line if called with default values was hidden because we didn't call it in a `finally` block.

This PR also fixes a quality issue in Jupyter where some of the `wandb.init()`​ status updates (like “creating run (\<duration>)”) would remain after the operation completed. This was because the code to clear the text was not in a `finally`​ block and was skipped when the asyncio task running it got cancelled.

The `progress_close()`​ method is probably unnecessary: its only effect is to close (hide) a progress bar widget in Jupyter, but we never display one. A progress bar is only displayed when `progress_update()`​ is used, but its only callsite is in `progress.py`​ in a codepath that can’t be reached in Jupyter as far as I can tell.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: improve asyncio_compat.open_task_group() (#10442)

Adds an optional timeout to `open_task_group()`​ (useful in a test in PR #10441), and a `race()`​ function.

Improves cancellation handling: it’s important to await tasks after calling `cancel()`​ to allow them to run their `finally`​ blocks. Otherwise, the `finally`​ blocks run sometime later, which could be unexpected, for example:

```
event = asyncio.Event()
cleaned_up = False

async def failing_task():
    await event.wait()
    raise ValueError

async def task_with_cleanup():
    try:
        event.set()  # allow failing_task() to fail
        ...          # do work
    finally:
        cleaned_up = True

async with asyncio_compat.open_task_group() as group:
    group.start_soon(failing_task())
    group.start_soon(task_with_cleanup())

# cleaned_up would have been False here before this PR
# until an await statement.
```

commit message:
feat: wire up `wandb beta sync` (#10453)

- `RunSyncer` syncs a single file
- `RunSyncOperation` represents multiple `RunSyncer` instances working together on one or more files that are part of a single `sync` command
- `RunSyncManager` puts it all together and handles the `sync` server requests

Since this is high-level logic, it’s tested primarily by `tests/system_tests/test_core/test_offline_sync_beta.py`​ rather than through unit tests.

After this PR, it's possible to sync using `wandb beta sync`, but there are some TODOs:

- This currently directs log messages to `debug-core.log` and doesn't configure Sentry
- `RunSyncer.Sync()`​ doesn’t relay errors back to the user (just logs them)
