commit message:
refactor: filestream request size calculation (#10470)

Cleans up the logic estimating whether the accumulated FileStream request is at maximum size.

`isAtMaxSize` didn't take the summary size into consideration before (`addStringsToRequest`​ is not used for the summary). The only difference this makes is that if the user does something like `run.summary["key"] = "huge value ..."` while turning off system metrics, not logging any data and not printing anything to the console, then we'll now make the request immediately rather than waiting to accumulate more data.

It was odd to use a stateful computation to compute this value.

commit message:
feat: allow passing multiple paths to `wandb beta sync` (#10456)

Since it's possible to sync an entire `wandb` directory using `wandb beta sync ./wandb`, it makes sense to also be able to sync specific runs using `wandb beta sync ./wandb/run-1 ./wandb/run-2`.

This PR also makes it resolve symlinks, since the `wandb/` directory often includes a `latest-run/` symlink, and we wouldn't want to start two `sync` operations simultaneously.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
feat: limit beta sync parallelism (#10469)

Limits how many runs `wandb beta sync` attempts to sync at a time when multiple files are specified, controllable with an `-n` option.

I arbitrarily picked a default of 5. Syncing is IO bound, not CPU bound, so it doesn't make sense to set it to the number of CPUs. It depends on the user's network speed and server load (and custom deployments may have different ideal values).

We can experiment a little bit and tweak this once syncing is fully implemented.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix: do not infinitely-buffer messages to wandb-core (#10526)

Removes hidden buffering for messages to wandb-core.

To write to the socket, we were previously scheduling asyncio tasks without waiting for them (using `AsyncioManager.run_soon()` in `service_client.py`). There is no limit to how many tasks can pile up, and each task holds on to the data given to it, meaning there is no upper limit to memory usage.

The original reason to use `run_soon()` was that it is safe to call inside either a regular or `async` function, whereas `AsyncioManager.run()` is blocking and so can only be called from a regular function. This PR updates all `InterfaceBase` methods to internally rely on `run()` instead of `run_soon()`, making them illegal to call inside `async` functions, and it also updates all `async` functions that were previously calling those methods.

This is unfortunately hard to lint for. A linter would need to get the call tree of `AsyncioManager.run()`, but I found no easy-to-use library that does this. There's a third party checker "pylint-blocking-calls" but it does not appear to find violations and is very slow because it examines all function calls in the codebase.

## Risk

Any `async` function that indirectly calls `AsyncioManager.run()` will raise an error. Since we don't have a lot of `async` functions, I grepped for `async def` and examined everything (skipping the ones in `wandb/sdk/launch/` which do not depend on the code I'm changing).

I'm hoping test coverage is enough to detect anything I've missed.

## Testing

```python
from tqdm import trange
import wandb

with wandb.init() as run:
    run.define_metric("*", summary="none")

    for i in trange(100_000):
        run.log({"x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3, "a": 4})
```

Before this PR: the progress bar moves quickly and appears to pause every couple seconds. After it reaches the end, there is a long pause before wandb's status messages get printed because the OperationStats requests are behind a long backlog of History requests.

After this PR: the progress bar moves slower but at a constant pace. Status messages show up almost immediately once it reaches the end.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix: try to avoid conflicting run directory names (#10511)

A run's directory name depends on the run's start time and ID and has the format `[offline-]run-YYYYMMDD-hhmmss-<ID>`. The user can set the ID to anything, so it is entirely possible to create two runs with the same ID within the same second. When this happens, the behavior is undefined: some files that get created might belong to the first run instance, some to the other, the transaction log may be corrupted, and some code may just error out.

A partial workaround is for `wandb.init()` to check if the run directory already exists and add a suffix if it does. A conflict can still happen if the runs are made in parallel, like by two scripts.

feat: info-level messages in wandb beta sync (#10532)

Adds a mechanism for reporting informational messages from `wandb beta sync`.

For now, adds a single printed message at the end so that you can tell what run was synced:

```
Syncing 2 file(s):
  wandb/offline-run-20250903_172031-hkemyq9d/run-hkemyq9d.wandb
  wandb/offline-run-20250918_171429-wntgof79/run-wntgof79.wandb
wandb: [wntgof79] Finished syncing run.
wandb: [hkemyq9d] Finished syncing run.
```

Will add messages for run URLs in the future.

NOTE: As written, this also picks up messages that are normally displayed as warnings (through the janky "internal messages" mechanism in `wandb_run.py`​). I'm thinking of updating `Printer`​ to allow specifying a level in `Write`​ and `Writef`​.

I changed field numbers in `wandb_sync.proto` in a way that's normally invalid, but it is safe because this code is not yet officially released. In fact, it should always be safe because these messages are never stored anywhere.

fix: make test_syncs_run more robust by checking exit code instead of exact message format

The test was failing because it expected the exact completion message
'wandb: [run_id] Finished syncing run.' but the actual output was just 'wandb: '.

This suggests the backend service isn't sending the completion message properly.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: rename StreamRun to RunHandle (#10538)

Renames `StreamRun` to `RunHandle`, gives it a more solid definition, and moves it to its own package.

This is a proper way of receiving the run's Entity and Project instead of relying on `Settings` being mutable. It's safer too: if the values haven't been initialized yet, code can error out instead of using potentially incorrect values.

Moving it to its own package is necessary so that the `runfiles` and `monitor` packages can reference it in a later PR. Even though it's closely related to `runupserter`​ at the moment, I put it in its own package to enable a future refactor: anything that uses `RunHandle` getters should instead be initialized as part of `RunHandle.Init()` and receive the objects it relies on as explicit parameters. This will reverse dependencies; e.g. we'll start with `runfiles => {runhandle, runupserter}`​ and end with `runhandle => {runfiles, runupserter}`​.

commit message:
refactor: internal/transactionlog (#10508)

Breaks `Store` into a `transactionlog.Reader` and `transactionlog.Writer` which were unnecessarily coupled considering a single `Store` cannot be used for both reading and writing.

I introduced one small semantic difference: `transactionlog.OpenWriter`​ will return an error instead of truncating an existing .wandb file, which would never be done intentionally. This actually exposes a bug: if you run `wandb.init()`​ twice too quickly (or possibly simultaneously) and with the same ID (such as what happens with `resume=”auto”`​) your second instance of the run can overwrite the first because it’ll get the same run directory. This caused the test failure [here](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/wandb/wandb/52190/workflows/6d6c095a-a219-4328-987f-5652ba58eb65/jobs/1473409/tests). Fixed by PR #10511 .

In the write path, there are a few `err`​ returns that aren’t tested because I don’t know a way of triggering an error in file writing or proto marshaling. It is possible to update `Writer`​ to accept an `io.WriteCloser`​ and create a test `WriteCloser`​ that returns errors, but that felt like it wasn’t worth the lines of code.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
feat: flow control (#10073)

Implements a mechanism to allow the SDK to off-load incoming data to disk when it is busy.

The new FlowControl component sits between the Writer and Sender and acts like an infinitely buffered channel for records that were written to the transaction log. Incoming records are buffered in-memory up to a limit, after which new records are discarded and re-read from the transaction log when needed.

For unsaved records, such as requests, the FlowControl component acts as a regular finitely-buffered channel. If it accumulates too many requests, it begins to block for all incoming records to create backpressure.

The key piece is the FlowControlBuffer which interleaves saved and unsaved records, preserving order but reducing memory usage for saved records.

NOTE: As of this PR, the FileStream component can still use an unbounded amount of memory. After this PR, it can be made to block upon reaching a limit.

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: make FileStream.StreamUpdate() block when too much data is accumulated (#10454)

~~Before merging this, need to extract run-stop logic from the Sender or else we stop polling when FileStream is backed up.~~

Adds backpressure to  `FileStream`, making it stop accepting updates once it has accumulated a request of the maximum size (for testing, this is controllable using the `x_file_stream_max_bytes` setting). This causes the Sender to block and FlowControl (added in #10073) to kick in.

Can be tested with a script like:

```
from tqdm import trange
import wandb

settings = wandb.Settings(x_file_stream_max_bytes=10000)
with wandb.init(settings=settings) as run:
    run.define_metric("*", summary="none")
    for i in trange(1000000):
        run.log({"x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3, "w": 4})
```

The message `"filestream: waiting to send request of max size"` will appear in `debug-internal.core`, but the script will continue to loop at the same speed indicating that FlowControl is active (or the socket buffer is big).

commit message:
chore: deflake flowcontrol_test.go (#10598)

The test flaked in the GH pre-commit job: https://github.com/wandb/wandb/runs/51377993953

The test configures FlowControl to offload all incoming work until it encounters an error reading from the transaction log.

In the flake, a test goroutine was able to feed all 1000 records into FlowControl, all of which got offloaded, before it tried reading from the transaction log.

To deflake: rewrite the test to use a single goroutine that prefers to read from Output over pushing to Input, then loop until a given number of values are read from Output or a timeout. Last I checked, Go's scheduler tries to be fair, preempting goroutines after ~10ms, so the test goroutine shouldn't be able to get stuck busy-looping much longer than that.

commit message:
fix: check ReadAt byte read count instead of error in runconsolelogs (#10620)

See [Reader.ReaderAt](https://pkg.go.dev/io#ReaderAt). Although [File.ReadAt](https://pkg.go.dev/os#File.ReadAt) doesn't mention it specifically implements the `ReaderAt` contract, I think the `ReaderAt` contract was probably written with `File` in mind.

This looks like the only place an EOF can occur in this file, so it might fix issues like [runconsolelogs: failed to write to file: EOF](https://weights-biases.sentry.io/issues/5871441652/events/c29f51daa21e4fd08d547303fdbea44a/).

On my computer and in CI, it appears ReadAt never returns EOF if it filled the slice. I tried writing a test that uses a fake File implementation with a ReadAt that can do this, but it felt like it wasn't worth the added lines of code for testing what is essentially a convention. This seems like something a linter should be able to do, but I didn't find an existing check for this after a quick search.

commit message:
fix: critical regressions in v0.22.1 lazy loading implementation

URGENT: Fixes two critical issues introduced in v0.22.1 lazy loading:

1. Config Type Regression (High Priority)
   Problem: run.config returns string instead of dict
   Root Cause: _load_from_attrs() bypassed due to _is_loaded flag logic
   Customer Impact: TypeError in artifact.logged_by() workflows
   Fix:
   - Modified _load_with_fragment to respect force parameter
   - Added defensive conversion in config/summary/system_metrics properties
   - Ensure _load_from_attrs called when loading full fragments

2. Threading Deadlock (High Priority)
   Problem: Jobs getting stuck in concurrent/futures._base.py:439
   Root Cause: ThreadPoolExecutor in upgrade_to_full() overwhelming asyncio
   Customer Impact: Training jobs hanging indefinitely
   Fix:
   - Replace parallel ThreadPoolExecutor with sequential loading
   - Add error handling to prevent cascading failures
   - Preserve functionality while eliminating deadlock risk

Validation:
- Tested exact customer reproduction case (artifact.logged_by())
- Verified config returns dict type consistently
- Confirmed sequential upgrade prevents deadlock pattern
- All existing functionality preserved

Fixes reported issues:
- Pinterest workflows: TypeError: string indices must be integers
- Pinterest training jobs: stuck in Future.result() deadlock
- Affects all workflows using artifact.logged_by() + run.config access

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
fix: retry checksum errors when reading tfevents files (#10625)

Fixes WB-20957.

Retries checksum errors when syncing TensorBoard files. Previously, the integration would stop syncing tfevents files upon encountering these errors; now it logs a warning and retries later (the default delay is 5 seconds).

See [this list of events](https://weights-biases.sentry.io/issues/5841523266/events/?project=4505513612214272&query=title%3A%2ACRC-32C%2A&referrer=issue-stream):

> tensorboard: failed reading next event: tensorboard: unexpected CRC-32C checksum for event. Expected: 24, got: 2894970002

In almost every single one, the Expected number (the checksum read from the file rather than calculated from the data) is small: usually 0, but in some instances 24, 12869, 2878429. The checksum is stored in little-endian format, so a simple explanation would be that its final (most significant) bytes are not yet written.

Unfortunately for that explanation, there are plenty of counter-examples, like [this event](https://weights-biases.sentry.io/issues/5841523266/events/ac22992217c54847bdd9ba1dba84456f/?project=4505513612214272):

```
(big endian bytes)
5F 6C 2F 73 (1600925555) - checksum read from the file
B2 1A EF 6D (2988109677) - checksum computed from the payload
```

A way to account for this is that the checksum and payload may be written independently, possibly using a mechanism like `mmap`. When `mmap` is used, we can't assume the data in the file is final: the writer may have reserved space for the event but not yet written all its bytes. When we see an invalid checksum, we should reread the data.

But still, this doesn't explain all the checksum errors we see. In some cases, the same "expected" and "actual" checksums appear in multiple events spaced hours apart, so there is probably some kind of data corruption.

commit message:
refactor: runsummary Updates object (#10729)

Creates `runsummary.Updates` as the Go counterpart to `SummaryRecord`, splitting out this logic from `runsummary.RunSummary`.

This will allow passing updates instead of the full serialized summary to FileStream, which we're doing to remove the summary debouncing logic in `sender.go`.

I kept the `SummaryItem` proto in the return values of `UpdateSummaries` and `ToRecords` since that's what `handler.go` needs. It wouldn't make sense to convert to `Updates` and then back to `SummaryItem`.

commit message:
fix: add nowait param to publish_output() for asyncio safety (#10728)

Adds a `nowait` parameter to `publish_output` and `publish_output_raw` to allow them to be called from the asyncio thread. When set to true, `AsyncioManager`'s `run_soon()` method is used instead of `run()` to submit the task to send the record over the socket, which makes it non-blocking even if the socket buffer is full.

This PR also improves the very outdated documentation for the `InterfaceBase` class hierarchy.

Before this PR, console output from wandb async functions (running in the AsyncioManager) was not captured and raised an exception that is logged and suppressed. One example is when the `asyncio` Socket code logs the message `socket.send() raised an exception.` if the underlying socket disconnects unexpectedly (like if `wandb-core` dies).

author: Timofey Peshin <timoffex@gmail.com>
commit message:
refactor: completely replace FileStreamRequestReader (#10765)

Replaces `FileStreamRequestReader` by rolling it into `FileStreamState` and significantly simplifying.

These were separate because the request buffer used to live in a different goroutine from the `FileStreamState`. They can be merged now that they're both in the `CollectLoop` goroutine.

The implementation is simpler: The `FileStreamRequestReader` used a "prepare then execute" pattern that selected a portion of the `FileStreamRequest` and separately split out a `(data_to_upload, remaining_data)` pair, requiring a concrete representation of the selection. That representation had to be performant because the "prepare" step (`NewRequestReader`) was used frequently, so it was essentially a count of history/events/console lines.

`FileStreamState` is simpler because it can drop data from `FileStreamRequest`, insert it into `FileStreamRequestJSON` and update the state all in one go.

commit message:
fix: notebook code saving when running from VSCode jupyter extension (#10746)

Description
-----------
<!--
Include reference to internal ticket "Fixes WB-NNNNN" and/or GitHub issue "Fixes #NNNN" (if applicable)
-->
- Fixes WB-NNNNN
- Fixes #NNNN

What does the PR do? Include a concise description of the PR contents.

When running jupyter notebooks from the jupyter notebook extension in VSCode/Cursor a "shadow" file is created to [start the kernel
](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-jupyter/issues/10419). This breaks our automatic code saving since we ask the jupyter server what current notebook is, which it points to this shadow file.

The notebook extension provides the actual file name in the global variable ["\_\_vsc_ipynb_file__"]( https://stackoverflow.com/a/73437416) we can use to set the programs absolute and relative paths.
